title: SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers

paper.title: SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full
pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost.
Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent
evaluations instead of recomputing them.
Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by accumulating a cheap
probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spending a fresh
evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching :
the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step,
fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size.
We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it
sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse.
We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching : instead of a binary
switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes.
Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step.
These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid.
SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on
HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times , it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity
metrics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow models set the state of the art in image and video synthesis ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . These models are slow at inference: producing a single output requires tens of full network evaluations, each a pass through the same large transformer. Yet the latent changes only slightly between steps, so successive passes largely recompute what the previous one already produced. This redundancy is the resource that acceleration methods draw on, and they differ in what they are willing to give up to reach it. In practice, this is done using distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Salimans & Ho, 2022 ) , fewer-step solvers ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , or cheaper attention ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) , each with its own cost in training, calibration, or fidelity. A different lever is to reuse the model’s own output, i.e., caching , instead of solving faster or attending more cheaply. Successive steps can then share computation directly rather than recompute it. Every cache must still decide when to refresh, and many settle this before sampling begins, with a refresh pattern that is fixed in advance and shared by every prompt ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Aliev et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic caches instead make refresh timing their central question and decide it during sampling: a cheap probe of the network predicts how much its output is about to change, and this signal decides, per prompt, when the cached computation has gone stale ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) . Yet these dynamic caches spend the signal on a single binary decision, a form of hard caching : at every node of the sampler’s fixed grid, the signal is compared with a threshold, and the sampler either reuses the cached computation or refreshes it. How far below the threshold the signal sits plays no role. A node where the cache has barely aged and one on the verge of refresh are treated identically, and both advance by exactly the step the schedule prescribed. x 0 x_{0} x 1 x_{1} true trajectory scheduled node refresh reuse cache off-grid landing SoftCache skips multiple scheduled nodes x 0 x_{0} x 1 x_{1} true trajectory scheduled node refresh reuse cache off-grid landing SoftCache skips multiple scheduled nodes Figure 1: SoftCache: how far, not just whether. Hard caching walks the fixed grid of scheduled nodes one node at a time, deciding only whether to refresh or reuse . SoftCache also sets the step size: a reused step the cache still supports skips several nodes and lands between them (inset). We observe that this ignored distance is informative. Below the threshold, the signal closely tracks the reuse error, the gap between the cached computation and a fresh one at the current node. The distance from the threshold, which we call the headroom , measures how safely the cache can be trusted, and we use it to set the step size instead of only the refresh decision: this is soft caching . When the headroom is large, the cache is still reliable, so the sampler takes a long step that skips several scheduled nodes and can land between them ( Fig. 1 ). When the headroom is small, refresh is near, so the step shrinks back toward the scheduled one. We call this method SoftCache: the headroom sets the step continuously rather than picking how many nodes to skip, and every node a step passes over is one the sampler no longer visits. Set against both kinds of cache, this is a different form of adaptivity. A fixed schedule refreshes at the same nodes for every prompt. A dynamic cache refreshes at nodes that vary with the prompt, but at scheduled nodes all the same. Here the steps vary with the prompt too, and they also land where no node was scheduled. This freedom translates into fidelity: on FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, against caches of both kinds at comparable speed, SoftCache reproduces the uncached model most faithfully on every metric at every operating point we test. Adaptivity, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh. It also decides where the sampler goes next. Our main contributions are: (1) We identify that the refresh signal of a dynamic cache carries more than a binary decision: its headroom below the threshold tracks the reuse error, so it measures how far the cached computation can still be trusted. (2) We propose SoftCache, which reads the headroom as a step size: cached steps jump off the scheduler’s grid in proportion to it, the tail is re-spaced so that every node passed is dropped from the trajectory, and the cached residual is extrapolated linearly to the landing, at no extra network cost. (3) On image and video backbones, SoftCache adds no per-backbone settings and is ahead of every cache we compare on all four fidelity metrics in every speed band from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times .

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion sampling acceleration
sections.text: Methods that cut sampling cost differ in what they modify. Some change the network or a single evaluation of it: distillation trains a student that needs fewer steps ( Song et al., 2023 ; Salimans & Ho, 2022 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) , while sparse attention ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) and token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2023 ) make each step cheaper. Others change the grid: higher-order solvers reach a given quality in fewer steps ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , and schedule design places the steps where they matter most ( Karras et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Sabour et al., 2024 ) . We work in a third family, caching, which changes neither the network nor an evaluation of it: it exploits the redundancy between neighboring states along the trajectory and reuses computation from earlier steps, without training.

sections.heading: 2.2 Feature caching
sections.text: Caching methods differ in what they store and when they refresh it. The stored quantity ranges from intermediate activations of U-Net or transformer blocks ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) to the residual of a span of blocks or of the entire stack ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) , and it may be refreshed for only a subset of tokens ( Zou et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) . Fixed schedules refresh periodically ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) or at steps chosen offline, by thresholding a reuse error calibrated on a few samples ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) or by optimizing for a fixed budget of full evaluations ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Aliev et al., 2026 ) . Online rules refresh once an accumulated cheap proxy of the output change crosses a threshold ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ; Nam et al., 2026 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . Such rules therefore refreshe at different nodes for different prompts, whereas a fixed schedule applies one refresh pattern to all of them. Either way, each node, or token, makes one binary choice between a full evaluation and reuse. SoftCache refreshes on the same spectral signal ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , but also reads its headroom below the threshold to make reuse soft rather than binary.

sections.heading: 2.3 Predictive caching
sections.text: Between refreshes, most caches hold the stored quantity fixed ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) , so the reuse error grows with the time since the last refresh. Predictive caches extrapolate from recent history instead. Some forecast what the network returns, the output of the block stack ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , its increment over the input ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , or the velocity itself ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Others forecast the increment each attention and MLP branch adds to its input, which the current node applies to its own activations, with Taylor ( Liu et al., 2025b ) or Hermite ( Feng et al., 2026 ) coefficients built from several stored past values. Multistep formulas ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025a ) and a check on the prediction ( Liu et al., 2025c ) extend how far it can be carried. All of them predict only at the nodes of the sampler’s schedule, so the schedule itself is untouched. We extrapolate an increment as well, a single one for the entire stack, along the straight line through the two most recent fresh evaluations. Written in the flow time, that line is defined between nodes, which is what lets the sampler leave the schedule rather than only skip evaluations along it.

sections.heading: 2.4 Adaptive step size control
sections.text: Adaptive ODE solvers set each step at runtime from an estimate of the local error, obtained by comparing two solutions of different order ( Dormand & Prince, 1980 ) , and the same control has been applied to diffusion sampling in both its SDE ( Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2021 ) and ODE ( Lu et al., 2022 ) forms. The estimate costs several network evaluations per step, which is the computation a cache exists to avoid. SoftCache takes its step size from the refresh signal the cache already computes, so the schedule adapts at no evaluations beyond those the cache spends anyway.

sections.text: Diffusion and flow models generate a sample by transporting noise to data along a differential equation. In diffusion models this is a reverse-time SDE or, equivalently, its probability-flow ODE, whose drift is built from a learned score ( Song et al., 2021b ) , while in flow matching the network regresses the transporting velocity directly ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2022 ) . sections.heading: 5.2 Image generation
sections.text: Tab. 1 reports four fidelity metrics at three matched speed bands on FLUX, Sec. B.1 adds latency, TFLOPs and peak memory, and Sec. B.2 resolves each band per prompt. SoftCache is ahead of every baseline on all four metrics in all three bands, and at the fastest band it leads SeaCache by 1.12 1.12 dB PSNR and 0.082 0.082 LPIPS. Because each method’s speed is set by its own parameter, a lead in quality could come from running slower. None of the leads above does. SoftCache is faster than SeaCache and DPCache in every band, and the only two runs faster than it, TeaCache at the slowest band by 0.23 × 0.23\times and TaylorSeer at the middle band by 0.15 × 0.15\times , trail it by 7.2 7.2 and 8.6 8.6 dB. Fig. 4 shows generation for three DrawBench prompts at the ≈ 5.2 × \approx\!5.2\times band, and illustrates what the gaps of Tab. 1 look like in the image. In these examples the baselines lose the structure of objects, not only their detail. In the first row two of them break the zebra itself, leaving it without a head (TeaCache) or with a second one (DPCache, red ellipses), and even SeaCache, the closest to SoftCache, loses the stripe pattern in the enlarged region, where black bleeds into the white stripes. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SoftCache, a training-free method that turns hard caching into soft caching. A dynamic cache already measures how stale its cached computation has become, but spends the measurement on a binary choice between refresh and reuse. SoftCache reads the headroom below the threshold as how far the cache can still be trusted and lets it set the step size: cached steps jump past scheduled nodes while the cache is reliable and shrink back to the scheduled step as a refresh nears, the tail is re-spaced so that every node passed is dropped from the trajectory, and the cached residual is extrapolated to each off-grid landing at no extra network cost. On FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, at wall-clock speedups from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times , SoftCache stays closest to the uncached sample on all four fidelity metrics, with no per-model calibration. Adaptivity in caching, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh.

sections.heading: A.3 Jump guards
sections.text: Eq. 9 stretches the step at every cached node, since a cached node has A i < τ A_{i}<\tau and therefore H i > 0 H_{i}>0 . Two guards override it and make the node take the scheduled step Δ i \Delta_{i} instead: the opening stretch, t i < 0.1 t_{i}<0.1 , and a large probe change at the node itself, ρ i > 0.18 \rho_{i}>0.18 with ρ i \rho_{i} as in Eq. 6 . The two thresholds are the same for every model and resolution in the paper. On FLUX at τ = 0.8 \tau=0.8 over 100 100 DrawBench prompts, 1,103 1{,}103 of the 5,000 5{,}000 scheduled nodes are cached but held to the scheduled step instead of jumping, 800 800 by the opening stretch, 302 302 by the large-change guard and one whose stretched step would be less than 1 % 1\% longer, which the sampler rounds to Δ i \Delta_{i} . Turning both guards off in Tab. C.4.2 leaves LPIPS within noise at every matched speed and moves PSNR by + 0.59 +0.59 dB at 3 × 3\times and − 0.66 -0.66 dB at 7 × 7\times .

sections.heading: A.4 Re-spacing geometry
sections.text: The rebuilt tail of Eq. 11 is spaced uniformly in t t . The alternative is to space it the way the backbone’s scheduler spaces its own grid. Diffusers schedulers build a grid from uniform points u u through the shift map w s ​ ( u ) = s ​ u / ( 1 + ( s − 1 ) ​ u ) w_{s}(u)=su/\big(1+(s-1)u\big) on the noise level 1 − t 1-t , with a shift s s fixed by the checkpoint ( s = e 1.15 s=e^{1.15} for FLUX at our resolution). Applying the same map to the tail gives 1 − t i + 1 + k = w s ( ( 1 − k m i − 1 ) w s − 1 ( 1 − t i + 1 ) ) , k = 0 , … , m i − 1 , 1-t_{i+1+k}=w_{s}\!\left(\Big(1-\frac{k}{m_{i}-1}\Big)\,w_{s}^{-1}\big(1-t_{i+1}\big)\right),\qquad k=0,\ldots,m_{i}-1, (13) which unwarps the landing node, spaces m i m_{i} nodes evenly between it and t = 1 t=1 , and warps them back. At s = 1 s=1 the map is the identity and Eq. 13 is Eq. 11 . On FLUX we compare the two on DPG-50 with the protocol of Sec. C.4 . They differ by at most 0.26 0.26 dB PSNR, at 3 × 3\times in favour of Eq. 11 , and the sign of the difference flips between speeds on PSNR and on the perceptual metrics alike. With no consistent winner we keep Eq. 11 on every backbone.

sections.heading: B.3 Reference-free metrics
sections.text: Our main tables measure fidelity to the uncached sample generated from the same noise and prompt, since a cache approximates the uncached sampler. Reference-free metrics instead judge a generated image or video by its own quality, independent of any other sample. We report two of them here, ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) for images and VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) for video. ImageReward (package 1.5 1.5 , ImageReward-v1.0 weights) scores human preference and prompt alignment. We score FLUX on DrawBench-200 for the uncached sampler and for every method of Tab. 1 at the ≈ 3.7 × \approx\!3.7\times and ≈ 5.2 × \approx\!5.2\times bands. ImageReward separates the methods only where the fidelity metrics already do. sections.heading: C.1 Headroom and reuse error
sections.text: Fig. 2 is measured on uncached FLUX trajectories, in the setting of Sec. A.1 , on 40 40 DrawBench prompts. Since nothing is reused, the residual is exact at every node. We can therefore pair every node with every later one, treating the earlier node as the anchor, which gives 1,128 1{,}128 pairs per prompt. For each pair we compute the reuse error E i E_{i} and the accumulator A i A_{i} . The first and last nodes are excluded as boundary effects. Panel (a) keeps the pairs a hard cache would reuse, those with A i A_{i} below the threshold, and plots their error against the accumulator. Error grows with the accumulator: a node about to trigger a refresh ( A i ≈ τ A_{i}\approx\tau ) has 2.2 × 2.2\times the median error of one just after a refresh ( A i ≈ 0 A_{i}\approx 0 ), although a threshold treats the two alike. This is the factor quoted in Sec. 4.1 . Since both the error and the accumulator grow with the distance from the anchor, we also check that A i A_{i} is more than a step counter: at a fixed gap i − a i-a of 2 2 to 12 12 nodes, A i A_{i} still orders the pairs by error with a Spearman correlation of about 0.8 0.8 , computed per prompt and averaged.

sections.text: SoftCache assumes nothing of the probe ρ i \rho_{i} of Eq. 6 beyond ρ i ≥ 0 \rho_{i}\geq 0 and the reset of A i A_{i} at a refresh, so either dynamic cache can host it. We use SeaCache’s filtered probe ( Chung et al., 2026 ) throughout. Here we swap in TeaCache’s polynomial-rescaled probe ( Liu et al., 2025a ) for both the refresh decision and the headroom, hold the rest of SoftCache fixed ( J = 8 J{=}8 , β = 1 \beta{=}1 , tail re-spacing, the τ \tau grid), and score both configurations at matched wall-clock budget against both caches on DPG-50 ( Tab. C.2.1 ). The policy transfers. sections.heading: C.3 Cap sweep and the blind-pick protocol
sections.text: The cap ladder of Tab. C.4.2 fixes J = 8 J{=}8 on DPG-50. Smaller caps ( J = 3 J{=}3 , J = 5 J{=}5 ) are perceptually worse from 5 × 5\times on. Larger caps are a wash through 5 × 5\times , gaining PSNR and giving it back on LPIPS and DreamSim, and win only at 7 × 7\times , where they lose high-frequency texture ( Sec. C.4 ). J = 8 J{=}8 is therefore the smallest cap that gives up nothing through 5 × 5\times . The 7 × 7\times band is handled by β \beta instead ( Sec. 5.4 ), which costs no texture. Two blind checks below back this, both on DPG-50 only. In each, one author saw, per prompt, the uncached reference and several unlabeled variants in a random order, with only the speedup shown.

sections.heading: Reject test at 𝟓 × 5\times .
sections.text: The six variants differ only in the cap, J ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 8 , 12 , 32 } J\in\{1,3,5,8,12,32\} , at matched ≈ 5 × \approx 5\times . The rater rejected any variant visibly worse than the reference, or marked the prompt “can’t tell”. The rule was fixed in advance: keep J = 8 J{=}8 if it has the lowest or tied-lowest reject rate, otherwise switch to the cap that is strictly lower. Five prompts were “can’t tell”. On the remaining 45 45 , J = 8 J{=}8 was never rejected ( 0 / 45 0/45 ), against 2 % 2\% for J = 3 J{=}3 and J = 5 J{=}5 , 22 % 22\% for J = 1 J{=}1 , 53 % 53\% for J = 12 J{=}12 and 91 % 91\% for J = 32 J{=}32 , so the rule keeps J = 8 J{=}8 .

sections.heading: D.1 What the fidelity metrics measure
sections.text: PSNR is a per-pixel error, so it rewards an output that drifts toward a smooth conditional mean and penalises one that keeps sharp detail slightly out of place. At high speedups a blurred output can therefore outscore a sharper one that looks closer to the reference. Fig. D.1.1 shows such a case. On one HunyuanVideo clip at a similar speedup, SeaCache leads SoftCache by 3.19 3.19 dB in PSNR, yet its foliage is visibly blurred (inset), and SSIM, LPIPS and DreamSim all favour SoftCache. We therefore report PSNR in every table but never decide on it alone, and we back the ablation choices with blind visual comparisons ( Sec. C.3 ). Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22369v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026 SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers Shimon Malnick Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Nadav Orenstein Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Ohad Fried Affiliation: Reichman University Project page: malnick.net/softcache Shai Avidan Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Abstract Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost. Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent evaluations instead of recomputing them. Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by accumulating a cheap probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spending a fresh evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching : the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching : instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step. These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid. SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times , it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity metrics. 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow models set the state of the art in image and video synthesis ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . These models are slow at inference: producing a single output requires tens of full network evaluations, each a pass through the same large transformer. Yet the latent changes only slightly between steps, so successive passes largely recompute what the previous one already produced. This redundancy is the resource that acceleration methods draw on, and they differ in what they are willing to give up to reach it. In practice, this is done using distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Salimans & Ho, 2022 ) , fewer-step solvers ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , or cheaper attention ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) , each with its own cost in training, calibration, or fidelity. A different lever is to reuse the model’s own output, i.e., caching , instead of solving faster or attending more cheaply. Successive steps can then share computation directly rather than recompute it. Every cache must still decide when to refresh, and many settle this before sampling begins, with a refresh pattern that is fixed in advance and shared by every prompt ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Aliev et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic caches instead make refresh timing their central question and decide it during sampling: a cheap probe of the network predicts how much its output is about to change, and this signal decides, per prompt, when the cached computation has gone stale ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) . Yet these dynamic caches spend the signal on a single binary decision, a form of hard caching : at every node of the sampler’s fixed grid, the signal is compared with a threshold, and the sampler either reuses the cached computation or refreshes it. How far below the threshold the signal sits plays no role. A node where the cache has barely aged and one on the verge of refresh are treated identically, and both advance by exactly the step the schedule prescribed. x 0 x_{0} x 1 x_{1} true trajectory scheduled node refresh reuse cache off-grid landing SoftCache skips multiple scheduled nodes x 0 x_{0} x 1 x_{1} true trajectory scheduled node refresh reuse cache off-grid landing SoftCache skips multiple scheduled nodes Figure 1: SoftCache: how far, not just whether. Hard caching walks the fixed grid of scheduled nodes one node at a time, deciding only whether to refresh or reuse . SoftCache also sets the step size: a reused step the cache still supports skips several nodes and lands between them (inset). We observe that this ignored distance is informative. Below the threshold, the signal closely tracks the reuse error, the gap between the cached computation and a fresh one at the current node. The distance from the threshold, which we call the headroom , measures how safely the cache can be trusted, and we use it to set the step size instead of only the refresh decision: this is soft caching . When the headroom is large, the cache is still reliable, so the sampler takes a long step that skips several scheduled nodes and can land between them ( Fig. 1 ). When the headroom is small, refresh is near, so the step shrinks back toward the scheduled one. We call this method SoftCache: the headroom sets the step continuously rather than picking how many nodes to skip, and every node a step passes over is one the sampler no longer visits. Set against both kinds of cache, this is a different form of adaptivity. A fixed schedule refreshes at the same nodes for every prompt. A dynamic cache refreshes at nodes that vary with the prompt, but at scheduled nodes all the same. Here the steps vary with the prompt too, and they also land where no node was scheduled. This freedom translates into fidelity: on FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, against caches of both kinds at comparable speed, SoftCache reproduces the uncached model most faithfully on every metric at every operating point we test. Adaptivity, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh. It also decides where the sampler goes next. Our main contributions are: (1) We identify that the refresh signal of a dynamic cache carries more than a binary decision: its headroom below the threshold tracks the reuse error, so it measures how far the cached computation can still be trusted. (2) We propose SoftCache, which reads the headroom as a step size: cached steps jump off the scheduler’s grid in proportion to it, the tail is re-spaced so that every node passed is dropped from the trajectory, and the cached residual is extrapolated linearly to the landing, at no extra network cost. (3) On image and video backbones, SoftCache adds no per-backbone settings and is ahead of every cache we compare on all four fidelity metrics in every speed band from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times . 2 Related Work 2.1 Diffusion sampling acceleration Methods that cut sampling cost differ in what they modify. Some change the network or a single evaluation of it: distillation trains a student that needs fewer steps ( Song et al., 2023 ; Salimans & Ho, 2022 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) , while sparse attention ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) and token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2023 ) make each step cheaper. Others change the grid: higher-order solvers reach a given quality in fewer steps ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , and schedule design places the steps where they matter most ( Karras et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Sabour et al., 2024 ) . We work in a third family, caching, which changes neither the network nor an evaluation of it: it exploits the redundancy between neighboring states along the trajectory and reuses computation from earlier steps, without training. 2.2 Feature caching Caching methods differ in what they store and when they refresh it. The stored quantity ranges from intermediate activations of U-Net or transformer blocks ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) to the residual of a span of blocks or of the entire stack ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) , and it may be refreshed for only a subset of tokens ( Zou et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) . Fixed schedules refresh periodically ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) or at steps chosen offline, by thresholding a reuse error calibrated on a few samples ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) or by optimizing for a fixed budget of full evaluations ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Aliev et al., 2026 ) . Online rules refresh once an accumulated cheap proxy of the output change crosses a threshold ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ; Nam et al., 2026 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . Such rules therefore refreshe at different nodes for different prompts, whereas a fixed schedule applies one refresh pattern to all of them. Either way, each node, or token, makes one binary choice between a full evaluation and reuse. SoftCache refreshes on the same spectral signal ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , but also reads its headroom below the threshold to make reuse soft rather than binary. 2.3 Predictive caching Between refreshes, most caches hold the stored quantity fixed ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Chung et al., 2026 ) , so the reuse error grows with the time since the last refresh. Predictive caches extrapolate from recent history instead. Some forecast what the network returns, the output of the block stack ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , its increment over the input ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , or the velocity itself ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Others forecast the increment each attention and MLP branch adds to its input, which the current node applies to its own activations, with Taylor ( Liu et al., 2025b ) or Hermite ( Feng et al., 2026 ) coefficients built from several stored past values. Multistep formulas ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025a ) and a check on the prediction ( Liu et al., 2025c ) extend how far it can be carried. All of them predict only at the nodes of the sampler’s schedule, so the schedule itself is untouched. We extrapolate an increment as well, a single one for the entire stack, along the straight line through the two most recent fresh evaluations. Written in the flow time, that line is defined between nodes, which is what lets the sampler leave the schedule rather than only skip evaluations along it. 2.4 Adaptive step size control Adaptive ODE solvers set each step at runtime from an estimate of the local error, obtained by comparing two solutions of different order ( Dormand & Prince, 1980 ) , and the same control has been applied to diffusion sampling in both its SDE ( Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2021 ) and ODE ( Lu et al., 2022 ) forms. The estimate costs several network evaluations per step, which is the computation a cache exists to avoid. SoftCache takes its step size from the refresh signal the cache already computes, so the schedule adapts at no evaluations beyond those the cache spends anyway. 3 Preliminaries Diffusion and flow models generate a sample by transporting noise to data along a differential equation. C.3 ). 6 Conclusion We presented SoftCache, a training-free method that turns hard caching into soft caching. A dynamic cache already measures how stale its cached computation has become, but spends the measurement on a binary choice between refresh and reuse. SoftCache reads the headroom below the threshold as how far the cache can still be trusted and lets it set the step size: cached steps jump past scheduled nodes while the cache is reliable and shrink back to the scheduled step as a refresh nears, the tail is re-spaced so that every node passed is dropped from the trajectory, and the cached residual is extrapolated to each off-grid landing at no extra network cost. On FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, at wall-clock speedups from 3.5 × 3.5\times to 6.9 × 6.9\times , SoftCache stays closest to the uncached sample on all four fidelity metrics, with no per-model calibration. Adaptivity in caching, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh. Acknowledgments This project was partially supported by ISF grants 1574/21 and 2132/23.
